_comment: DimensionCanon — real-world canonical dimensions for generated objects, in CUBES (1 cube = 1 m). Sibling of character_design_constraints.json. Furniture HEIGHTS are anthropometric (body-derived, period-stable, character-bounded); TYPES/footprints are medieval. Every archetype carries a primary `source` + a per-value `sources` map (the grounding rule). 'INFERRED' = reasonable estimate, low confidence; 'POST-MEDIEVAL' = anachronistic for the medieval frame, flagged. See docs/structure-generation/StructureGenerationV2.md + docs/structure-generation/StructureBrief.md.
_units: cubes (metres). 'tol' = tolerance in cubes. 'anchors' = required interaction-point ids.

keg.description: Tapped serving cask (kilderkin) laid on a stillage behind the bar
keg.source: English brewery cask units — kilderkin = 18 imperial gallons (Wikipedia, English brewery cask units); envelope DERIVED from that volume, not a product spec

sources.volume: kilderkin = 18 imp gal = 18 x 4.54609 L = 81.83 L = 0.08183 m3 (Wikipedia, English brewery cask units). The kilderkin (half-barrel) is the standard TAPPED serving cask, distinct from the storage 'barrel' archetype.
sources.diameter: DERIVED, not measured: cask volume ~= 0.86 * (pi/4) * d^2 * h (0.86 = the taper from bilge to head), holding the 1.6 h:d proportion the sibling 'barrel' archetype measures (0.89 h / 0.56 d = 1.59). Solving 0.08183 = 0.86 * 0.7854 * 1.6 * d^3 gives d = 0.423 m. ARITHMETIC from a cited volume + a measured sibling proportion — flagged DERIVED, not a cooper's spec.
sources.length: = the cask's own height, 1.6 x diameter = 0.68 m; it becomes LENGTH (and WIDTH, the placer's across-the-front extent) because a tapped cask lies horizontal (see orientation).
sources.height: = cask_diameter 0.42 + stillage_top 0.11 = 0.53 m. This archetype measures the object AS PLACED — cask resting on its chocks — because that is what the conformance audit compares against the emitted geometry.
sources.depth: = cask_diameter 0.42 m — the cross-section of a cask lying on its side.
sources.orientation: REASONED from the tap, not attested by a cited plan: a cask is broached and served horizontally so the tap sits at the low bilge and sediment settles below it — hence stillage/chocks. The upright form is the STORAGE pose ('barrel'). No medieval taproom plan was sourced for the gantry arrangement.
sources.stillage_top: STYLIZED — 1 micro (0.111 m) of chock, the smallest carvable rise that keeps the cask off the floor. No dimensioned stillage source.

hanging_sign.description: Projecting pictorial trade sign on a wrought-iron bracket, hung over a shop entrance
hanging_sign.source: modern historic-district / projecting-sign code (clearance, area, projection are safety/anthropometric); the medieval FORM = a pictorial board on a wrought-iron bracket over the entrance, clearing head height

sources.ground_clearance: projecting signs must clear >= 8 ft = 2.44 m above grade (Santa Clara UT 17.45.120, VERIFIED text: '>= 8 ft of ground clearance') -- anthropometric (clears head/horse), period-invariant. NOTE: some modern codes are STRICTER (Salt Lake City Ord. 61/2000 = 10 ft / 3.05 m; UK conservation shopfront guidance ~2.3-2.4 m); 2.44 m sits at/above the common 8 ft minimum. (grounding-auditor 2026-06-28: removed an incorrect 'SLC >= 8 ft' sub-cite (SLC is 10 ft) and an unsourced '2.6 m'.)
sources.board_w: board sized so total area <= 12 sq ft = 1.11 m2 cap (Santa Clara UT / typical historic projecting-sign area limit); 0.8 x 0.6 = 0.48 m2 is well under
sources.board_h: see board_w; 0.6 m board height keeps area 0.48 m2 < 1.11 m2 cap
sources.board_thick: GRID-SNAP: a real sawn plank sign board is ~1-2 in / 25-50 mm (a carved board to ~3 in / 75 mm); snapped UP to the microcube floor 1/9 m = 0.111 m (one block, the minimum representable), so the rendered board is ~0.04-0.09 m thicker than a real plank -- a disclosed grid snap, not a grounded thickness
sources.projection: projecting sign extends <= 48 in = 1.22 m from the building face incl. bracket (Santa Clara UT 17.45.120; common historic limit); 0.8 m arm is within it
sources._note: POST-MEDIEVAL CODE / PERIOD FORM: the numeric clearance/area/projection limits are modern sign-ordinance values (disclosed), but they are safety/anthropometric and the medieval principle is identical -- hanging pictorial trade signs on wrought-iron brackets over the street are well attested (illiterate clientele; size/projection regulation began 16th-18th c., e.g. 1669 French order, 1762-73 London). The PICTORIAL IMAGE itself = the DECAL system (backlog), not faked; this archetype is the BOARD + BRACKET geometry only, in existing materials (Wood board, Metal/Log bracket).
